newsitem.title: USA: You're buying credit life, but why?.
newsitem.headline: You're buying credit life, but why?.

text.p: The credit life insurance industry, those people who sell you coverage on your credit cards and car loans, are crowing. They're selling more insurance than ever, and collected $2.41 billion in premiums in 1995.
The real question is why? Consumer advocates maintain that credit life insurance tends to be more expensive, more restrictive and less likely to be collected on than basic life insurance.
"This thing is a rip off," concludes Peter Katt, a fee-only insurance advisor in Mattawan, Mich.

According to the Consumer Credit Insurance Association, the average cost of a credit life policy is 54 cents per $100 of coverage. That makes it as expensive as term life insurance for a 45-year-old smoker who's in bad health, says Katt.
Some policies, which insure credit card debt, can cost even more as they roll in coverage for unemployment and disability and bill consumers automatically in their credit card bills.
Pay your balances in full, and why do you need insurance? Fail to pay them in full, and you're paying interest every month on your insurance premium, too.

Morever, most credit life policies restrict the use of the benefit to paying off the loan in question. So, if you're buying a big credit life policy on a home mortgage, for example, and you die, your spouse may not have the option of putting the benefit in the bank and doling out the mortgage money.
Who buys these products? Unfortunately, they are most popular at lower ends of the education and income scales.
In a 1994 study of credit life insurance, Purdue University researchers found it most popular with those who had household income under $20,000.

Perhaps, as the credit life industry claims, these consumers might not be able to afford term life insurance, and want to be sure their heirs don't get stuck with bills. But the low income also might indicate that credit life buyers are retirees who have low income but enough assets to pay for their debts without shelling out such high rates for life insurance.

Does this mean you should never buy credit life insurance? Well, even Katt concedes that there's always a story to sell any insurance product: One individual whose family was saved because he bought a policy just in time. But the odds of a credit life policy being a smart or useful purchase are very slim, and this is not a wise way to spend your insurance dollars, especially if they are limited.

If you have heirs who depend on you for current income, and they won't be able to replace that income with the assets you might will them, then you need life insurance. It's best to buy a straight life insurance policy that pays a death benefit of 5 percent to 6 percent of your salary, and not worry about smaller policies on cancers and car loans.

If all you are worried about is covering your outstanding debts and your own funeral, remember that a 45-year-old non-smoker can buy a $50,000 term life insurance policy for about $85 a year, says Katt. Your family could use the proceeds as they see fit.
